t: What Docker Is and Why AI Developers Containerize
title: What Docker Is and Why AI Developers Containerize
description: Docker packages an application with its libraries, runtimes, and settings into a container — an isolated box that runs identically on any machine. For AI work this is transformative: a PyTorch + CUDA + Ollama stack that took a day to configure becomes a single image anyone can run. Docker Desktop brings this to Windows and Mac with a GUI, while Linux uses the engine directly.

t: Images vs Containers: The Core Distinction
title: Images vs Containers: The Core Distinction
description: An image is the frozen template (the recipe); a container is a running instance of it (the meal). Images are built from Dockerfiles, stored in registries, and versioned by tag. Containers start, stop, and are deleted — their writable layer is ephemeral unless you mount volumes. The discipline: images immutable, containers disposable, data in volumes.

demo.program:
print("IMAGE: frozen template (Dockerfile -> registry, versioned by tag).")
print("CONTAINER: running instance (start/stop/delete, ephemeral).")
print("Discipline: images immutable, containers disposable, DATA IN VOLUMES.")
print("Delete a container freely; never store data only in its writable layer.")

t: Docker Desktop: GUI, Engine, and Resource Controls
title: Docker Desktop: GUI, Engine, and Resource Controls
description: Docker Desktop bundles the Docker engine, a dashboard GUI, Docker Compose, and Kubernetes on Windows/Mac — running Linux containers via a lightweight VM (WSL2 backend on Windows). Its key organizer feature is resource control: sliders cap CPU, memory, and disk for all containers, so a runaway training job cannot freeze the host. It is free for personal use and small business.

print("Key organizer: resource sliders cap CPU/RAM/disk for ALL containers.")
print("Runaway training job can't freeze host: limits enforced.")
print("Free for personal + small business.")

t: Your First Container: Hello World to Useful
title: Your First Container: Hello World to Useful
description: The first commands: 'docker run hello-world' proves the engine works; 'docker run -it ubuntu bash' drops you in a Linux shell. The flags that matter: -d (detached), -p (port map, host:container), -v (volume mount), --name, --gpus all (NVIDIA). Learn these five flags and you can run nearly any AI image published anywhere.

demo.program:
print("docker run hello-world        # prove engine works")
print("docker run -it ubuntu bash    # interactive shell")
print("Flags that matter: -d -p host:ct -v host:ct --name --gpus all")
print("Five flags + any published AI image = running workload.")

title: Dockerfiles: Building Your Own Images
description: A Dockerfile is the recipe: FROM a base image, RUN install steps, COPY your code, CMD the startup command. Each instruction becomes a cached layer — unchanged layers reuse cache, so rebuilds are fast. For AI: start FROM nvidia/cuda, pip install torch, copy your training script. Keep images lean: one purpose per image, .dockerignore to exclude junk.

demo.program:
dockerfile = ["FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04", "RUN pip install torch --index-url cu124",
              "COPY train.py /app/", "WORKDIR /app", 'CMD ["python", "train.py"]']
print("Dockerfile (each line = cached layer):")
for line in dockerfile:
    print(f"  {line}")
print("Lean rule: one purpose/image, .dockerignore excludes junk.")

title: Docker Compose: Multi-Container AI Stacks
description: Compose orchestrates several containers as one stack via a YAML file — e.g., an Ollama LLM server plus an Open WebUI frontend plus a Postgres vector store, all networked, started with one command. This is how local AI workspaces are organized: the compose file IS the architecture, versioned in git, reproducible on any machine with 'docker compose up'.

demo.program:
compose = {"services": ["ollama (LLM server, GPU)", "open-webui (frontend)", "pgvector (embeddings)"],
           "command": "docker compose up -d", "file": "compose.yaml (git-versioned)"}
print("Stack:", ", ".join(compose["services"]))
print("Architecture as code:", compose["file"], "->", compose["command"])
print("Reproducible on ANY machine: the compose file is the system.")

t: Use Case: PyTorch + CUDA Training Environment
title: Use Case: PyTorch + CUDA Training Environment
description: The canonical AI container: NVIDIA's PyTorch image (torch + CUDA + cuDNN prebuilt) with your code volume-mounted and --gpus all passed through. Your host stays clean — no CUDA toolkit installs, no driver conflicts — and teammates run the identical stack. Dataset on a volume, checkpoints written back to the volume: the container holds compute, the volume holds value.

demo.program:
print("docker run --gpus all -v ./data:/data -v ./ckpt:/ckpt nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:24.01-py3")
print("Host: clean (no CUDA installs). Teammates: identical stack.")
print("Container = compute. Volumes = data + checkpoints (the value).")

t: Use Case: Ollama in Docker for Local LLMs
title: Use Case: Ollama in Docker for Local LLMs
description: Ollama containerized gives a local LLM API server with GPU passthrough: pull the image, run with --gpus all, volume-mount the model store so downloads persist, and 'ollama pull llama3' inside. Every app on your machine — and every teammate's — hits the same localhost:11434 API. Models persist in the volume; the container is replaceable.

demo.program:
print("docker run -d --gpus all -v ollama:/root/.ollama -p 11434:11434 ollama/ollama")
print("Then: docker exec <ct> ollama pull llama3.1")
print("API at localhost:11434 for every app. Models in volume, container disposable.")

t: Volumes and Bind Mounts: Data That Survives
title: Volumes and Bind Mounts: Data That Survives
description: Volumes (Docker-managed storage) and bind mounts (host paths mapped in) are how data outlives containers. Rule: code and datasets via bind mounts (edit on host, run in container), databases and model stores via named volumes (managed, portable). Back up volumes with 'docker run --volumes-from'. Data loss stories are always 'I kept it in the container'.

demo.program:
print("Bind mount (-v ./code:/app): edit on host, run in container. CODE + DATASETS.")
print("Named volume (-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql): managed + portable. DBs + MODELS.")
print("Back up: docker run --volumes-from. Data-loss stories = kept it in container.")

t: Resource Limits: Keeping the Host Alive
title: Resource Limits: Keeping the Host Alive
description: AI containers will eat every resource offered — set limits: '--memory 16g --cpus 8' on run, or deploy.resources in compose. Docker Desktop's global sliders are the backstop. GPU memory has no Docker limit (NVIDIA's --gpus passes the whole GPU) — manage VRAM inside the workload (batch sizes, model quantization). Limits are how the host survives the experiment.

demo.program:
print("docker run --memory 16g --cpus 8 ...  (per-container caps)")
print("Compose: deploy.resources.limits. Desktop: global sliders = backstop.")
print("GPU VRAM: NO docker limit (--gpus = whole GPU). Manage inside: batch/quantize.")
print("Limits = how the host survives the experiment.")

t: Networking: Ports, Networks, and Service Discovery
title: Networking: Ports, Networks, and Service Discovery
description: Containers on the same compose network reach each other by service name ('http://ollama:11434') — no IPs needed. Publish ports to the host only for what you use (-p 8080:8080). Custom networks isolate stacks from each other. For AI work: one network per project stack keeps the LLM, UI, and database cleanly connected and everything else out.

demo.program:
print("Same network: services reach by NAME (http://ollama:11434). No IPs.")
print("Publish (-p) only what you use. One network per project stack.")
print("LLM + UI + DB connected; everything else isolated.")

t: Image Hygiene: Pruning, Tags, and Disk Space
title: Image Hygiene: Pruning, Tags, and Disk Space
description: Docker eats disk: dangling images, stopped containers, unused volumes accumulate gigabytes. The hygiene: 'docker system prune' (with care), 'docker image prune', volume prune for the truly unused. Tag your images meaningfully (project:date, not just latest) — 'latest' is a lie in production. A monthly prune keeps the 100GB Docker disk from filling.

demo.program:
print("Eats disk: dangling images + stopped containers + unused volumes = GBs.")
print("Monthly: docker system prune (careful), image prune, volume prune.")
print("Tag meaningfully (proj:2026-10-21), not 'latest'. 'Latest' lies in production.")

t: Docker Desktop vs Native Engine vs Podman
title: Docker Desktop vs Native Engine vs Podman
description: Docker Desktop: GUI + easy, Windows/Mac standard, license terms for large business. Native engine (Linux): fastest, no VM overhead, CLI-native — the server choice. Podman: daemonless, rootless by default, Docker-compatible CLI — the security-conscious alternative. For AI dev on Windows/Mac: Desktop. On Linux servers: native engine. The compose files work across all three.

title: Troubleshooting: The Five Fixes
description: Most Docker problems are five things: port already in use (change -p), out of disk (prune), GPU not visible (--gpus all + nvidia runtime), volume permission denied (user/UID mapping), and 'works on my machine' (pin image tags, rebuild --no-cache). Learn to read 'docker logs' first — the answer is usually in the last twenty lines.

demo.program:
print("1. port in use -> change -p | 2. disk full -> prune")
print("3. no GPU -> --gpus all + nvidia runtime | 4. perms -> UID mapping")
print("5. works-on-mine -> pin tags, rebuild --no-cache")
print("Always first: docker logs (answer in last 20 lines).")

title: The Complete Docker Organization Discipline
description: The master discipline: one compose file per project stack (git-versioned), images pinned by tag, data in volumes, resources limited, networks per stack, monthly pruning, Desktop sliders as backstop, and the host kept clean of AI dependencies. The entire AI workspace becomes reproducible infrastructure — new machine, same 'docker compose up', same results.
